name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q01 - Anatomical discovery of the organ of Corti

questiontext.text: The Italian anatomist Alfonso Corti is primarily known in auditory physiology for discovering the organ of Corti located on which structure of the inner ear?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the scientist and structure from historical physiological context.
Alfonso Corti published a paper in 1851 describing the sensory receptor organ for hearing.

Step 2: Recall the specific anatomical location.
The organ of Corti contains hair cells that convert sound vibrations into nerve impulses and is located on the basilar membrane of the cochlea.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The structure supporting the organ of Corti is the basilar membrane.

questiontext.text: Which group of organisms exchanges \(\mathrm{O_2}\) with \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) by simple diffusion over their entire body surface?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze respiratory mechanisms across different animal phyla.
Lower invertebrates lack specialized vascularized respiratory organs because of their simple body plans and high surface-area-to-volume ratios.

Step 2: Relate to textbook examples.
Sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms utilize simple diffusion across their entire body surface for gas exchange.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Sponges, coelenterates, and flatworms carry out gas exchange over the whole body surface.

questiontext.text: Match the organism with its primary mode of respiration: earthworms respire through moist cuticle, while aquatic molluscs respire using:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify respiratory structures in aquatic molluscs.
Aquatic arthropods and molluscs possess vascularized structures called gills for respiration in water.

Step 2: Contrast with other forms.
Respiration through gills is termed branchial respiration, whereas earthworms exhibit cutaneous respiration and terrestrial forms use vascularized bags called lungs.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Gills (branchial respiration) are used by aquatic molluscs.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q04 - Level of tracheal bifurcation in humans

questiontext.text: In the human respiratory tract, the trachea is a straight tube extending up to the mid-thoracic cavity, which divides into a right and left primary bronchus at the level of the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Trace the anatomy of the human trachea.
The trachea descends through the neck into the thoracic cavity.

Step 2: Recall the exact vertebral landmark.
At the level of the 5th thoracic vertebra (T5), the trachea divides into right and left primary bronchi.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The bifurcation occurs precisely at the 5th thoracic vertebra.

questiontext.text: Incomplete cartilaginous rings provide structural support up to which section of the human respiratory tract?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify all airway passages that possess cartilaginous rings.
The trachea, primary bronchi, secondary bronchi, and tertiary bronchi are reinforced by cartilage to prevent collapse.

Step 2: Determine where cartilage rings terminate.
Cartilaginous rings extend up to the initial bronchioles; terminal bronchioles and alveoli lack cartilaginous support.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Incomplete cartilaginous rings support the passages up to the initial bronchioles.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is NOT a physiological function of the conducting part of the human respiratory system?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define the conducting zone of the respiratory system.
The conducting part extends from external nostrils up to the terminal bronchioles.

Step 2: List its designated functions.
It clears air of foreign particles, humidifies incoming air, brings air to body temperature, and transports air to the alveoli.

Step 3: Contrast with the exchange zone.
The actual diffusion of gases between blood and atmospheric air occurs exclusively across the exchange part (alveoli and their ducts).

Step 4: State the final conclusion.
Actual diffusion of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) across the capillary barrier is not a function of the conducting part.

answer.text: Serving as the site for actual diffusion of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) into blood
Clearing inhaled air of foreign particulate matter
Bringing the temperature of inhaled air to body temperature

questiontext.text: The human thoracic chamber is anatomically an air-tight cavity bounded:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify anatomical boundaries of the thoracic cage.
The cavity is bounded dorsally by the vertebral column, ventrally by the sternum, laterally by the ribs, and on the lower side by the dome-shaped diaphragm.

Step 2: Verify directional terminology.
Dorsal corresponds to the spine/vertebral column; ventral corresponds to the breastbone/sternum; lateral refers to the rib cage.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The boundaries are dorsally by vertebral column, ventrally by sternum, laterally by ribs, and inferiorly by the diaphragm.

answer.text: Dorsally by vertebral column, ventrally by sternum, laterally by ribs, and lower side by diaphragm
Dorsally by sternum, ventrally by vertebral column, laterally by ribs, and lower side by diaphragm
Dorsally by ribs, ventrally by clavicle, laterally by sternum, and lower side by abdominal muscles
Dorsally by vertebral column, ventrally by diaphragm, laterally by sternum, and lower side by ribs

questiontext.text: During normal quiet inspiration in humans, contraction of the diaphragm leads to an increase in thoracic cavity volume along which anatomical axis?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand how the diaphragm changes position during inspiration.
The relaxed diaphragm is dome-shaped. Contraction flattens it, pulling it downward toward the abdominal cavity.

Step 2: Relate downward displacement to the anatomical axis.
This downward flattening increases the thoracic cavity dimension in the antero-posterior axis.

Step 3: Contrast with intercostal muscle action.
Contraction of external intercostals lifts ribs and sternum, expanding the dorso-ventral axis.

Step 4: State the final conclusion.
The diaphragm increases thoracic volume along the antero-posterior axis.

questiontext.text: Contraction of external intercostal muscles contributes to inspiration by lifting the ribs and sternum, which increases thoracic volume in the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the action of external intercostal muscles.
These muscles pull the rib cage outward and upward, lifting both the ribs and the sternum.

Step 2: Determine the axis of thoracic enlargement.
Lifting the sternum away from the vertebral column enlarges the thoracic chamber in the dorso-ventral axis.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The increase occurs in the dorso-ventral axis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q10 - Physical condition for atmospheric air influx

questiontext.text: Inspiration occurs when which physical pressure relationship exists between the lungs and the atmosphere?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the pressure gradient required for fluid/gas flow.
Gases flow from regions of higher pressure to regions of lower pressure.

Step 2: Relate to intra-pulmonary and atmospheric pressures.
In order for atmospheric air to be drawn into the pulmonary cavity, intra-pulmonary pressure must fall below atmospheric pressure (creating negative pressure relative to atmosphere).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Intra-pulmonary pressure must be negative relative to atmospheric pressure.

answer.text: Intra-pulmonary pressure is less than atmospheric pressure
Intra-pulmonary pressure is equal to atmospheric pressure
Intra-pleural pressure becomes strictly positive with respect to atmospheric pressure

questiontext.text: Normal quiet expiration in humans is predominantly a passive process brought about by the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the mechanics of resting expiration.
Under resting conditions, expiration does not require active muscular contraction.

Step 2: Identify the muscle states.
Relaxation of both the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles returns the ribs, sternum, and diaphragm to their resting positions, decreasing pulmonary volume.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Quiet expiration results from the relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles.

answer.text: Relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles
Contraction of internal intercostal and abdominal muscles
Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals

questiontext.text: To enhance the strength and depth of expiration during forceful breathing, humans recruit additional muscles located in the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand forced breathing mechanics.
Normal quiet expiration is passive, but forceful expiration requires active muscular compression.

Step 2: Identify the accessory muscular groups.
Additional muscles present in the abdomen (and internal intercostals) contract to push the diaphragm upward and pull ribs downward.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Additional muscles in the abdomen are recruited to increase expiratory force.

questiontext.text: Under resting conditions, an average healthy adult human breathes at a rate of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the standard physiological breathing rate in healthy humans.
Under basal resting conditions, respiratory rhythm centre drives regular cyclical ventilation.

Step 2: State the textbook range.
The average respiratory rate is 12 to 16 breaths per minute.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The physiological breathing rate is 12–16 times/minute.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q14 - Total hourly ventilation from tidal volume

questiontext.text: If a healthy individual has a resting tidal volume of \(500\text{ mL}\) and breathes \(14\text{ times per minute}\), what is the total volume of air inspired in one hour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate minute respiratory volume.
\(\text{Minute volume} = \text{Tidal Volume} \times \text{Breaths per minute} = 500\text{ mL} \times 14 = 7000\text{ mL/min} = 7\text{ L/min}\).

Step 2: Convert minute ventilation into hourly ventilation.
\(\text{Hourly volume} = 7000\text{ mL/min} \times 60\text{ min} = 420{,}000\text{ mL} = 420\text{ L}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The total air volume inspired in one hour equals \(420\text{ L}\) (or \(420{,}000\text{ mL}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q15 - Typical range for inspiratory reserve volume

questiontext.text: The additional volume of air that a healthy human can inspire by a forcible inspiration (Inspiratory Reserve Volume, IRV) averages:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV).
IRV is the extra volume of air an individual can inhale beyond normal tidal inspiration.

Step 2: Recall standard clinical physiological values.
The average range given in standard human physiology is \(2500\text{ mL}\) to \(3000\text{ mL}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The average IRV is \(2500\text{ mL}\) to \(3000\text{ mL}\).

questiontext.text: The volume of air that remains inside the lungs even after the most strenuous, forcible expiration is termed:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define the volume of gas that cannot be exhaled.
Lungs never collapse entirely during breathing; a cushion of gas is retained inside the alveoli and airways.

Step 2: Match with standard terminology.
This volume is called Residual Volume (RV) and averages \(1100\text{ mL}\) to \(1200\text{ mL}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The air remaining after forcible expiration is Residual Volume.

questiontext.text: A spirometry test shows a person's Tidal Volume (\(\mathrm{TV}\)) is \(500\text{ mL}\) and Inspiratory Reserve Volume (\(\mathrm{IRV}\)) is \(2800\text{ mL}\). What is this individual's Inspiratory Capacity (\(\mathrm{IC}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Recall the definition and formula for Inspiratory Capacity.
Inspiratory Capacity is the total volume of air a person can inhale after a normal expiration: \(\mathrm{IC} = \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\).

Step 2: Substitute the given clinical values.
\(\mathrm{IC} = 500\text{ mL} + 2800\text{ mL} = 3300\text{ mL}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The Inspiratory Capacity is \(3300\text{ mL}\).

questiontext.text: Functional Residual Capacity (\(\mathrm{FRC}\)) represents the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a normal expiration and is mathematically equal to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the state of the lungs following normal quiet expiration.
After a normal expiration, the lungs still contain the air that could be voluntarily pushed out plus the air that cannot be exhaled at all.

Step 2: Combine the relevant respiratory volumes.
The volume remaining is Expiratory Reserve Volume (\(\mathrm{ERV}\)) plus Residual Volume (\(\mathrm{RV}\)), so \(\mathrm{FRC} = \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Functional Residual Capacity equals \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q19 - Definition and components of vital capacity

questiontext.text: Vital Capacity (\(\mathrm{VC}\)) of the human lung is correctly represented by which combination of respiratory volumes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Define Vital Capacity.
Vital Capacity is the maximum volume of air a person can breathe in after a forced expiration (or breathe out after a forced inspiration).

Step 2: Identify the components.
It comprises Expiratory Reserve Volume (\(\mathrm{ERV}\)), Tidal Volume (\(\mathrm{TV}\)), and Inspiratory Reserve Volume (\(\mathrm{IRV}\)).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Vital Capacity is \(\mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{TV} + \mathrm{IRV}\).

questiontext.text: Which pulmonary volume or capacity CANNOT be measured directly using a standard spirometer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the mechanism of spirometry.
A spirometer measures the volume of air moved into and out of the respiratory tract during breathing movements.

Step 2: Identify volumes that cannot be moved into the spirometer.
Residual Volume (\(\mathrm{RV}\)) cannot be exhaled under any circumstance. Consequently, any capacity containing \(\mathrm{RV}\)—such as Functional Residual Capacity (\(\mathrm{FRC}\)) and Total Lung Capacity (\(\mathrm{TLC}\))—cannot be measured directly with a spirometer.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Residual Volume cannot be measured directly using a spirometer.

questiontext.text: If a person has a Vital Capacity of \(4600\text{ mL}\) and a Functional Residual Capacity of \(2300\text{ mL}\), with an Expiratory Reserve Volume of \(1100\text{ mL}\), what is their Total Lung Capacity (\(\mathrm{TLC}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate Residual Volume (\(\mathrm{RV}\)) from Functional Residual Capacity.
\(\mathrm{FRC} = \mathrm{ERV} + \mathrm{RV} \implies \mathrm{RV} = \mathrm{FRC} - \mathrm{ERV} = 2300\text{ mL} - 1100\text{ mL} = 1200\text{ mL}\).

Step 2: Compute Total Lung Capacity (\(\mathrm{TLC}\)).
\(\mathrm{TLC} = \mathrm{VC} + \mathrm{RV} = 4600\text{ mL} + 1200\text{ mL} = 5800\text{ mL}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The Total Lung Capacity is \(5800\text{ mL}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q22 - Oxygen partial pressure in alveolar air

questiontext.text: What are the partial pressures of oxygen (\(p\mathrm{O_2}\)) and carbon dioxide (\(p\mathrm{CO_2}\)) respectively in alveolar air under standard physiological conditions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Review alveolar gas partial pressures.
In alveolar air, constant gas exchange with pulmonary blood lowers \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) and raises \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) compared to ambient air.

Step 2: State the standard values from Table 14.1.
Alveolar air has a \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) of \(104\text{ mm Hg}\) and a \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) of \(40\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The partial pressures are \(104\text{ mm Hg}\) and \(40\text{ mm Hg}\) respectively.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q23 - Partial pressure values in deoxygenated blood

questiontext.text: In systemic venous (deoxygenated) blood entering the pulmonary circulation, the values of \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Analyze gas partial pressures in systemic venous blood.
Deoxygenated blood returns from metabolically active tissues where oxygen is extracted and carbon dioxide is added.

Step 2: Recall textbook values.
In deoxygenated blood, \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) is \(40\text{ mm Hg}\) and \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) is \(45\text{ mm Hg}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The values are \(p\mathrm{O_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\) and \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 45\text{ mm Hg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q24 - Carbon dioxide solubility and diffusion rate

questiontext.text: The solubility of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in blood and tissue fluids is how many times higher than that of \(\mathrm{O_2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the solubility factor affecting gas diffusion.
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to gas solubility through the respiratory membrane.

Step 2: Recall the exact comparative solubility ratio.
The solubility of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is 20 to 25 times higher than that of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The solubility of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) is 20–25 times higher than that of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q25 - Layers of the alveolar diffusion membrane

questiontext.text: The diffusion membrane across which respiratory gas exchange occurs consists of which three microscopic layers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the anatomical barriers separating alveolar air from capillary blood.
Gases must cross the alveolar wall, an intervening extracellular matrix, and the blood vessel wall.

Step 2: Name the specific histological layers.
These are: (1) thin squamous epithelium of the alveoli, (2) endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and (3) the intervening basement substance supporting both cellular layers.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The three layers are squamous epithelium of alveoli, capillary endothelium, and the basement substance between them.

answer.text: Squamous epithelium of alveoli, endothelium of alveolar capillaries, and basement substance between them
Ciliated columnar epithelium, smooth muscle layer, and capillary endothelium
Cuboidal epithelium of alveoli, tunica media, and capillary basement membrane
Pseudostratified epithelium, pleural fluid layer, and endothelial lining

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q26 - Total thickness of the diffusion membrane

questiontext.text: The total thickness of the human alveolar-capillary diffusion membrane is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the structural adaptation for efficient diffusion.
Fick's law of diffusion dictates that the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to membrane thickness.

Step 2: Recall the textbook dimension.
The combined thickness of all three layers of the diffusion membrane is much less than a millimetre (\(\ll 1\text{ mm}\), roughly \(0.2\text{ to }0.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\)).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The thickness is much less than a millimetre.

questiontext.text: In human blood, oxygen is transported in two forms. The respective percentages transported by red blood cells and dissolved in plasma are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify oxygen transport mechanisms in blood.
Oxygen has low solubility in aqueous solutions, requiring a chemical carrier.

Step 2: Quantify the two modes.
About 97 percent of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is transported bound to haemoglobin in RBCs, while the remaining 3 percent is carried in a dissolved state through plasma.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The percentages are 97% by RBCs and 3% dissolved in plasma.

answer.text: 97% by RBCs and 3% dissolved in plasma
70% by RBCs and 30% dissolved in plasma
80% by RBCs and 20% dissolved in plasma
50% by RBCs and 50% dissolved in plasma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q28 - Forms and percentages of carbon dioxide transport

questiontext.text: Which option correctly details the percentages of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) transported as bicarbonate, carbamino-haemoglobin, and in dissolved state through plasma?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify all three modes of carbon dioxide transport.
Carbon dioxide is carried as bicarbonate ions (\(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\)), bound to amine groups of haemoglobin, and dissolved directly in plasma.

Step 2: Recall textbook percentages for each mode.
Bicarbonate accounts for about 70%, carbamino-haemoglobin accounts for 20–25%, and dissolved state in plasma accounts for about 7%.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The correct values are 70% as bicarbonate, 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin, and 7% dissolved in plasma.

answer.text: 70% as bicarbonate, 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin, 7% dissolved in plasma
97% as bicarbonate, 3% as carbamino-haemoglobin, 0% dissolved in plasma
20–25% as bicarbonate, 70% as carbamino-haemoglobin, 7% dissolved in plasma
50% as bicarbonate, 40% as carbamino-haemoglobin, 10% dissolved in plasma

questiontext.text: Each molecule of human haemoglobin possesses four iron-containing haeme groups and can bind reversibly with a maximum of how many molecules of \(\mathrm{O_2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the quaternary structure of haemoglobin.
Haemoglobin is a tetramer consisting of four globin subunits, each containing one ferrous (\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\)) haeme moiety.

Step 2: Relate binding capacity to haeme groups.
Each haeme group binds one diatomic oxygen molecule (\(\mathrm{O_2}\)), allowing a single haemoglobin molecule to carry up to four molecules of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Haemoglobin can carry a maximum of four molecules of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q30 - Conditions favouring oxyhaemoglobin formation in alveoli

questiontext.text: Which set of physiological conditions at the alveolar surface favours the formation of oxyhaemoglobin?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify factors affecting haemoglobin-oxygen affinity.
Oxygen loading is favoured by high substrate availability and conditions that stabilize the relaxed (R) state of haemoglobin.

Step 2: Evaluate alveolar conditions.
In pulmonary alveoli, there is high \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), low \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration (higher pH), and lower temperature.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
High \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), lesser \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and lower temperature favour oxyhaemoglobin formation.

answer.text: High \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), lesser \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and lower temperature
Low \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), high \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and higher temperature
High \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), high \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and lower temperature
Low \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), lesser \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and higher temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q31 - Factors promoting oxygen unloading at tissues

questiontext.text: At the level of metabolically active peripheral tissues, oxygen dissociates from oxyhaemoglobin primarily because of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine peripheral tissue microenvironment.
Cellular respiration consumes oxygen and generates carbon dioxide, heat, and metabolic acids.

Step 2: Relate microenvironment to haemoglobin affinity.
Low \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), high \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and elevated temperature decrease haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, promoting dissociation.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Low \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), high \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and higher temperature drive oxygen dissociation.

answer.text: Low \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), high \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and higher temperature
High \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), low \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and lower temperature
High \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), high \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), low \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and higher temperature
Low \(p\mathrm{O_2}\), low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), low \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration, and lower temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q32 - Shape of the oxygen haemoglobin dissociation curve

questiontext.text: When the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is plotted against the partial pressure of oxygen (\(p\mathrm{O_2}\)), the resulting curve exhibits a:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand haemoglobin allosteric cooperative binding.
Binding of the first oxygen molecule increases the affinity of the remaining haeme subunits for oxygen.

Step 2: Identify the mathematical curve shape.
This cooperative binding mechanism generates a characteristic S-shaped or sigmoid curve.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
A sigmoid curve is obtained.

questiontext.text: Under normal resting physiological conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of oxygenated blood delivers approximately how much \(\mathrm{O_2}\) to the tissues?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Determine oxygen content of systemic blood.
\(100\text{ mL}\) of fully oxygenated blood carries approximately \(19.4\text{ to }20\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

Step 2: Determine tissue extraction under resting conditions.
Venous blood leaving resting tissues remains roughly 75% saturated, carrying about \(14\text{ to }15\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) per \(100\text{ mL}\).

Step 3: Calculate the delivered volume.
The net quantity delivered to tissues is approximately \(5\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) per \(100\text{ mL}\) of blood.

Step 4: State the final conclusion.
Every \(100\text{ mL}\) of oxygenated blood delivers approximately \(5\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

questiontext.text: Under normal resting conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately how much \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) to the pulmonary alveoli?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand carbon dioxide transport and unloading.
Deoxygenated blood carries carbon dioxide collected from active tissues back to the lungs.

Step 2: Recall the physiological delivery value.
Under resting conditions, every \(100\text{ mL}\) of deoxygenated blood delivers approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) into the alveoli.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The volume delivered is approximately \(4\text{ mL}\) of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).

questiontext.text: The zinc-containing metalloenzyme carbonic anhydrase facilitates the reversible conversion of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) into carbonic acid. This enzyme is found in:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the cellular distribution of carbonic anhydrase in blood.
Red blood cells require extremely rapid interconversion of dissolved \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and bicarbonate ions during transit through capillaries.

Step 2: Contrast RBC concentration with plasma.
RBCs contain a very high concentration of carbonic anhydrase, whereas plasma contains only minute quantities of the enzyme.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Very high concentration is present in RBCs, with minute quantities in plasma.

answer.text: Very high concentrations in RBCs and minute quantities in plasma
High concentrations in plasma and completely absent in RBCs
Platelets only, being absent in both RBCs and plasma

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q36 - Primary neural centre governing respiratory rhythm

questiontext.text: The primary specialised neural centre primarily responsible for maintaining and regulating the basic respiratory rhythm in humans is located in the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify brainstem centres controlling ventilation.
The brainstem contains rhythm generators and regulatory modulating centres.

Step 2: Distinguish the primary rhythm generator.
The respiratory rhythm centre is located in the medulla oblongata and is primarily responsible for basic cyclical breathing movements.

Step 3: Contrast with the pons.
The pneumotaxic centre in the pons modulates the rhythm centre rather than generating the primary rhythm.

Step 4: State the final conclusion.
The primary centre is situated in the medulla region of the brain.

questiontext.text: The pneumotaxic centre is situated in the pons region of the brain. Its primary regulatory action on the respiratory rhythm centre is to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the modulatory role of the pneumotaxic centre.
Neural signals transmitted from the pneumotaxic centre switch off inspiration.

Step 2: Determine the effect on respiratory rate.
By reducing the duration of inspiration, it prevents lung over-inflation and increases the respiratory frequency.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Signals from the pneumotaxic centre reduce the duration of inspiration and thereby alter respiratory rate.

answer.text: Reduce the duration of inspiration and alter the respiratory rate
Prolong the duration of inspiration and cause hypoventilation
Directly monitor oxygen concentration in the arterial blood
Stimulate relaxation of abdominal muscles during forced expiration

questiontext.text: The chemosensitive area situated adjacent to the medullary respiratory rhythm centre is highly sensitive to increases in which chemical species?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify chemical stimuli for central respiratory control.
The central chemosensitive area detects changes in cerebrospinal fluid and surrounding interstitial fluid chemistry.

Step 2: Recall specific chemical triggers.
It responds with high sensitivity to elevated \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and hydrogen ions (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)), signaling the rhythm centre to stimulate ventilation.

Step 3: Contrast with oxygen sensitivity.
The role of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) in the direct regulation of respiratory rhythm is considered insignificant.

Step 4: State the final conclusion.
The chemosensitive area is sensitive to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and hydrogen ions.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q39 - Insignificant role of oxygen in rhythm regulation

questiontext.text: In the physiological regulation of resting respiratory rhythm in humans, the direct sensory role of which factor is considered quite insignificant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluate relative roles of blood gases in respiratory drive.
Ventilatory drive is dominated by feedback from central and peripheral chemoreceptors responding to hypercapnia (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)) and acidosis (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)).

Step 2: Note the textbook assertion on oxygen.
The role of oxygen in regulating normal respiratory rhythm is quite insignificant.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Oxygen plays an insignificant role in regulating respiratory rhythm.

questiontext.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors capable of recognizing changes in arterial \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration to modulate respiratory output are located in the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify arterial vascular structures housing chemosensory bodies.
Receptors monitoring circulating blood composition are located at strategic major arterial sites.

Step 2: Recall the specific anatomical locations.
Sensory receptors associated with the aortic arch and carotid artery detect elevations in \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) and transmit afferent signals to the respiratory rhythm centre.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Receptors are located in the aortic arch and carotid artery.

questiontext.text: Asthma is a respiratory disorder characterized clinically by wheezing and difficulty in breathing due to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the primary pathophysiology of asthma.
Asthma involves hypersensitivity of the lower airways.

Step 2: Connect pathology to clinical symptoms.
Inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles causes airway narrowing, spasms, and wheezing during breathing.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The symptom complex is caused by inflammation of bronchi and bronchioles.

answer.text: Fibrous proliferation in the upper nasal mucosa
Loss of surfactant in terminal alveolar ducts

questiontext.text: A chronic respiratory disorder often caused by cigarette smoking in which the alveolar walls are damaged and the respiratory surface is significantly decreased is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify chronic obstructive pathology linked to smoking.
Chronic exposure to cigarette smoke irritates alveolar septa and triggers enzymatic breakdown of elastic fibres.

Step 2: Match damage pattern to disease name.
The destruction of alveolar walls resulting in reduced gas exchange surface area is diagnostic of emphysema.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The disorder described is emphysema.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q43 - Chronic stone dust exposure and fibrosis

questiontext.text: In occupational respiratory disorders associated with stone-breaking and grinding industries, chronic dust inhalation leads to lung damage primarily through:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand the physiological effect of prolonged mineral dust inhalation.
Excess silica or mineral dust overwhelms alveolar macrophage defense mechanisms.

Step 2: Identify the histological outcome.
Persistent irritation triggers chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous connective tissue) and irreversible loss of lung elasticity.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Damage occurs via chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissues).

answer.text: Chronic inflammation leading to fibrosis (proliferation of fibrous tissues)
Acute bacterial infection of tracheal cartilaginous rings
Excessive accumulation of pleural fluid causing pleural friction
Direct chemical destruction of the epiglottic cartilage

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q44 - Directional gas gradients across alveolar membrane

questiontext.text: Consider the partial pressures of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) in alveoli (\(p\mathrm{O_2} = 104\text{ mm Hg}\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\)) and systemic deoxygenated blood (\(p\mathrm{O_2} = 40\text{ mm Hg}\), \(p\mathrm{CO_2} = 45\text{ mm Hg}\)). The resulting concentration gradients drive:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Calculate the pressure gradient for oxygen.
Alveolar \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) (\(104\text{ mm Hg}\)) is higher than blood \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) (\(40\text{ mm Hg}\)), driving \(\mathrm{O_2}\) from alveoli into blood.

Step 2: Calculate the pressure gradient for carbon dioxide.
Deoxygenated blood \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) (\(45\text{ mm Hg}\)) exceeds alveolar \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) (\(40\text{ mm Hg}\)), driving \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from blood into alveoli.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
Diffusion of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) occurs from alveoli to blood and diffusion of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) occurs from blood to alveoli.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{O_2}\) from alveoli into blood and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from blood into alveoli
\(\mathrm{CO_2}\) from alveoli into blood and \(\mathrm{O_2}\) from blood into alveoli

questiontext.text: During the process of swallowing, entry of food into the larynx is prevented by the closure of the glottis by which structure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the anatomical opening to the airway.
The glottis is the opening of the larynx.

Step 2: Identify the protective cartilaginous flap.
A thin, elastic cartilaginous flap called the epiglottis folds over the glottis during swallowing to divert food into the oesophagus.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The glottis is covered by the epiglottis.

answer.text: A thin elastic cartilaginous flap called epiglottis

questiontext.text: When bicarbonate-rich blood arrives at the pulmonary capillaries where \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) is low, carbonic anhydrase facilitates the formation of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Examine the chemical equilibrium of carbonic anhydrase.
\(\mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightleftharpoons{} \mathrm{H_2CO_3} \xrightleftharpoons{} \mathrm{HCO_3^-} + \mathrm{H^+}\).

Step 2: Determine reaction direction at low \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\).
At the alveolar site where \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) is low, the equilibrium shifts to the left: \(\mathrm{HCO_3^-}\) and \(\mathrm{H^+}\) combine to form carbonic acid, which rapidly cleaves into \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\).

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The reaction leads to the release of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q47 - Right shift of oxygen dissociation curve

questiontext.text: A rightward shift of the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin signifies a decreased affinity for oxygen. Which condition causes this rightward shift?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Understand what causes a right shift in the oxygen dissociation curve.
A rightward shift indicates that a higher \(p\mathrm{O_2}\) is required to achieve 50% saturation, meaning oxygen affinity is reduced (Bohr effect).

Step 2: Identify allosteric factors promoting right shift.
Increased \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\), increased \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration (decreased pH), elevated temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG promote right shift and oxygen release.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
High \(p\mathrm{CO_2}\) and high \(\mathrm{H^+}\) concentration shift the curve to the right.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BREATHINGANDEXCHANGEOFGASES_MCQ_Q48 - Pleural membrane layers and fluid function

questiontext.text: The human lungs are enclosed by a double-layered pleura with pleural fluid between them. Which statement correctly identifies the anatomical relationship of these layers?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identify the two layers of the pleura.
The lungs are surrounded by an outer parietal pleural membrane and an inner visceral pleural membrane.

Step 2: Describe their specific contacts and fluid role.
The outer pleural membrane remains in close contact with the thoracic lining, whereas the inner pleural membrane is in intimate contact with the lung surface. Pleural fluid between them reduces friction during respiratory excursions.

Step 3: State the final conclusion.
The outer pleura contacts the thoracic lining and the inner pleura contacts the lung surface.

answer.text: The outer pleural membrane is in contact with the thoracic lining, whereas the inner pleural membrane contacts the lung surface
The inner pleural membrane is in contact with the ribs, whereas the outer membrane contacts the alveolar basement
Both pleural membranes directly adhere to the pericardium without enclosing fluid
The outer pleural membrane lines the tracheal cartilages while the inner membrane lines the sternum
